title: What happens end to end when a Java program runs (javac → bytecode .class → JVM class loading → bytecode verification → runtime memory areas → JIT compilation of hot bytecode to native code → execution), and why is the JVM not just an interpreter?
shortTitle: What happens end to end when a Java program runs

s1_definition.profdef: When a Java program runs, source code is first compiled by `javac` into platform-neutral bytecode stored in `.class` files. At runtime the JVM loads these classes through its class loaders, verifies the bytecode for safety, allocates runtime memory areas such as the heap, the method area, and per-thread stacks, and then begins execution. The execution engine starts by interpreting bytecode but profiles it, and the Just-In-Time compiler compiles frequently executed "hot" methods into optimized native machine code, so the JVM is a hybrid interpreter-plus-compiler, not a pure interpreter.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India processing Rajesh's transfer. First an engineer writes the rulebook in English and a translator converts it into a standard coded form that any branch can read — that is `javac` producing bytecode. When a branch actually processes transfers, a supervisor first reads each coded instruction one at a time (interpretation). But the supervisor notices that the "debit then credit" steps happen thousands of times a day, so she prints a laminated fast-reference card with those steps pre-translated into direct actions (JIT native code). After that, those common steps run instantly without re-reading the rulebook. The JVM behaves exactly like that supervisor who starts slow but gets faster on the busy paths.
s1_definition.oneliner: Java source becomes bytecode once, then the JVM loads, verifies, interprets, and JIT-compiles the hot paths into native code — interpret first, compile the busy parts.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When a Java program runs, source code is first compiled by `javac` into platform-neutral bytecode stored in `.class` files. At runtime the JVM loads these classes through its class loaders, verifies the bytecode for safety, allocates runtime memory areas such as the heap, the method area, and per-thread stacks, and then begins execution. The execution engine starts by interpreting bytecode but profiles it, and the Just-In-Time compiler compiles frequently executed "hot" methods into optimized native machine code, so the JVM is a hybrid interpreter-plus-compiler, not a pure interpreter.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India processing Rajesh's transfer. First an engineer writes the rulebook in English and a translator converts it into a standard coded form that any branch can read — that is `javac` producing bytecode. When a branch actually processes transfers, a supervisor first reads each coded instruction one at a time (interpretation). But the supervisor notices that the "debit then credit" steps happen thousands of times a day, so she prints a laminated fast-reference card with those steps pre-translated into direct actions (JIT native code). After that, those common steps run instantly without re-reading the rulebook. The JVM behaves exactly like that supervisor who starts slow but gets faster on the busy paths.

**One line to remember:** Java source becomes bytecode once, then the JVM loads, verifies, interprets, and JIT-compiles the hot paths into native code — interpret first, compile the busy parts.

sections.s2_technical:
The journey begins with `javac`. It reads `TradeService.java` and produces `TradeService.class`. The `.class` file holds bytecode, which is a compact instruction set for the abstract JVM, not for any real CPU. This is why the same `.class` runs on Windows, Linux, or Mac.

At runtime the `java` launcher creates a JVM. The class loader subsystem then loads classes lazily, when they are first referenced. There are three standard loaders working as a delegation chain: the bootstrap loader for core classes, the platform loader for standard extensions, and the application loader for your own classes on the classpath. Loading has three phases: loading the bytes, linking (which itself is verification, preparation, and resolution), and initialization (running static initializers).

Verification is a critical safety step. The verifier confirms the bytecode does not violate JVM rules, for example that it does not forge object references, overflow the stack, or jump to invalid instructions. This is why you cannot sneak malicious handcrafted bytecode past the JVM.

Then memory areas are set up. The heap holds all objects, such as every `Account` and `BigDecimal` instance, and is shared across threads. The method area, implemented as Metaspace in modern HotSpot, holds class metadata and the runtime constant pool. Each thread gets its own JVM stack holding stack frames for method calls, its own program counter, and possibly native method stacks.

Execution starts in the interpreter, which reads bytecode one instruction at a time. The interpreter is quick to start but slow to run repeatedly. HotSpot profiles how often methods and loops run. When a method crosses a threshold it becomes "hot," and the JIT compiler compiles it into native machine code, applying optimizations like inlining, escape analysis, and dead code elimination. HotSpot has two JIT compilers, C1 for fast startup and C2 for aggressive optimization, used together in tiered compilation. A senior nuance is that the JIT can make speculative optimizations based on observed behavior and then deoptimize back to interpreted mode if an assumption breaks. This is why the JVM is not just an interpreter and why a long-running banking server can match or beat native C in some workloads.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank runs an interest calculation for millions of accounts every night. The very first few calculations are a little slow, but after a while the same calculation runs blazingly fast. The team wonders why. This is exactly how the JVM's interpret-then-JIT model works — the first runs are interpreted, then the hot method gets compiled to native code and speeds up.

Problem 2 — A security auditor worries that someone could hand-edit a `.class` file to bypass the balance check. This is exactly what bytecode verification prevents — the JVM refuses to run malformed or unsafe bytecode.

Problem 3 — Operations wants to prove that running the same calculation method many times triggers JIT compilation. This is exactly what we demonstrate by looping an interest calculation enough times to cross the compilation threshold and observing the speed-up.

The code has an `Account`, an `InterestCalculator` with a hot `calculateInterest` method, and a `NightlyBatch` main class that runs the calculation many times and measures how the per-call time drops as the JIT kicks in.

```
jvm-lifecycle-demo/

│   └── main/java/com/bank/runtime/
```

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile source into bytecode
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/runtime/NightlyBatch.java

# Run and ask the JVM to print when it JIT-compiles methods
java -XX:+PrintCompilation -cp out com.bank.runtime.NightlyBatch

# See the bytecode the verifier will check before running
javap -c -cp out com.bank.runtime.InterestCalculator
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's balance of 1,000,000 rupees, an annual rate of 3.5 percent, and 200,000 repeated calculations.

Step 1: `javac` compiles `NightlyBatch.java` into bytecode `.class` files on disk. Nothing has run yet.

Step 2: The `java` launcher starts the JVM. The application class loader loads `NightlyBatch`, and lazily loads `Account` and `InterestCalculator` when they are first used.

Step 3: The verifier checks each loaded class's bytecode is safe before any instruction executes.

Step 4: Memory areas are prepared. The `Account` object and each `BigDecimal` live on the shared heap. The loop variables and stack frames for `calculateInterest` live on the main thread's stack. Class metadata lives in Metaspace.

Step 5: Execution begins in the interpreter. The first several thousand calls to `calculateInterest` are interpreted one bytecode instruction at a time, which is relatively slow.

Step 6: HotSpot's profiler notices `calculateInterest` is extremely hot. The JIT compiler compiles it to optimized native code with inlining. The remaining calls now run as native instructions, dramatically faster per call.

Step 7: The final interest value and the total elapsed time are logged. The total time reflects a slow interpreted warm-up followed by fast native execution.

```text
INFO: Ran interest calc 200000 times
INFO: Interest per run for SAV2001 = 2916.67
INFO: Total time ms (interpret warmup + JIT native) = 41
```

```text
    │ javac
    ▼
  .class bytecode ──→ [JVM starts]
    │
    ▼

    ▼

    │
    ▼
  Runtime Memory Areas
    ├─ Heap        → Account, BigDecimal objects

    │
    ▼
  Execution Engine
    ├─ Interpreter (first ~N calls, slow)
    │        │ profiler marks method HOT
    │        ▼
    └─ JIT (C1→C2 tiered) → native code (fast)
    │
    ▼
  Output: interest = 2916.67 per run
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When a Java program runs, it passes through a well-defined end-to-end lifecycle. First, the compiler javac turns my source code into platform-neutral bytecode stored in class files. This bytecode is not machine code for any real processor; it is instructions for the abstract Java Virtual Machine, and that is what makes Java portable.

At runtime, the java launcher starts the JVM, and the class loader subsystem loads my classes lazily, the first time each is referenced, using a delegation chain of the bootstrap, platform, and application loaders. Before any code runs, the bytecode verifier checks that the loaded classes are safe and well-formed, which is a genuine security guarantee because it stops hand-crafted malicious bytecode from forging references or corrupting the stack.

The JVM then sets up its runtime memory areas: the shared heap where all objects like my Account and BigDecimal instances live, the method area or Metaspace for class metadata, and a private stack for each thread holding its method call frames. Execution begins in the interpreter, which runs bytecode one instruction at a time.

The key insight is that the JVM is not just an interpreter. HotSpot continuously profiles the running code, and when a method or loop becomes hot, the Just-In-Time compiler compiles it to optimized native machine code, using tiered compilation with the C1 and C2 compilers and optimizations like inlining and escape analysis. It can even make speculative optimizations and deoptimize if an assumption turns out to be wrong.

I saw this directly in our nightly interest batch at the bank. The first few thousand interest calculations were slightly slow while interpreted, and then the per-call time dropped sharply once the calculation method was JIT-compiled. That is why a long-running banking server actually gets faster the longer it runs, and why describing the JVM as a pure interpreter is incorrect.
